claims.text: The HEA is a homogeneous, disordered solid solution containing multiple principal elements.
The random distribution of multiple alloying elements produces atomic-level lattice distortions in the HEA.
Intrinsic lattice distortions intermittently trap or pin dislocations.
Intermittent dislocation pinning and release caused by lattice distortion produces dynamic strain aging.
Dislocation pinning increases the apparent strength of the HEA during cyclic or high-rate loading.
Eventual dislocation release and dynamic recovery preserve ductility during cyclic or high-rate loading.
The pinning effect is amplified at higher strain rates because dislocations have less time to overcome the obstacles.
The HEA should have higher strain-rate sensitivity than a conventional-alloy baseline matched for quasi-static strength and ductility.
Rapid loading should produce a larger flow-stress increase in the HEA than in the conventional-alloy baseline.
The HEA should maintain its ductility or show only a moderate ductility reduction while its strength increases.
The proposed behavior should occur primarily in the temperature regime where dynamic strain aging is active.
A sufficiently high strain rate is required to trigger the proposed intermittent-pinning effect.
The mechanism may cease to govern at very high temperatures because thermal activation dominates.
The mechanism may cease to govern at extremely low strain rates because equilibrium recovery can negate pinning.
Dynamic strain aging is a well-known mechanism in certain alloys.
Transformation-induced plasticity could contribute concurrently to the observed dynamic behavior.
The controlled comparison should use HEA and conventional-alloy samples having comparable static mechanical properties while holding geometry, environment, and preprocessing equivalent.
Failure to observe higher strain-rate sensitivity or intermittent dislocation pinning in the HEA relative to the control would falsify the proposed mechanism.
